danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 21
paragraphs: De russiske tropper passerede gennem Moskva fra klokken to om natten til klokken to om eftermiddagen og førte de sårede og de sidste af de afrejsende indbyggere med sig.
Den største trængsel under troppernes bevægelse fandt sted ved Sten-, Moskva- og Jauzabroerne.

Mens tropperne, der delte sig i to dele ved passagen rundt om Kreml, trængtes på Moskva- og Stenbroerne, benyttede et stort antal soldater sig af stoppet og trængslen til at vende om fra broerne og snige sig stille og ubemærket forbi Vasilij den Saliges kirke og under Borovitskij-porten, tilbage op ad bakken til Den Røde Plads, hvor et instinkt fortalte dem, at de let kunne tage ting, der ikke tilhørte dem. Menneskemasser som ved et billigsalg fyldte alle gangene og stræderne i Basaren. Men der var ingen handlende med indsmigrende, venlige stemmer, der indbød kunder til at komme indenfor; der var ingen gadehandlere og heller ikke den sædvanlige brogede skare af kvindelige kunder — kun soldater i uniformer og kapper, men uden geværer, der gik ind i Basaren tomhændede og tavst fandt vejen ud gennem gangene med bylter. Handlende og deres medhjælpere, som der kun var få af, bevægede sig rundt blandt soldaterne, helt forvirrede. De låste deres butikker op og låste dem igen og bar selv varer bort med hjælp fra deres medhjælpere. På pladsen foran Basaren stod trommeslagere og slog til samling. Men trommehvirvlen fik ikke de plyndrende soldater til at løbe i retning af trommen, som tidligere, men fik dem tværtimod til at løbe længere væk. Blandt soldaterne i butikkerne og gangene kunne man se mænd i grå frakker med tætklippede hoveder. To officerer, den ene med et sjal over uniformen og ridende på en mager, mørkegrå hest, den anden i kappe og til fods, stod på hjørnet af Iljinkagaden og talte sammen. En tredje officer kom galoperende hen til dem.
»Generalen befaler, at de alle skal drives ud med det samme, ufortøvet. Det er en skandale! Halvdelen af mændene er løbet deres vej.«
»Hvor skal I hen?... Hvor?...« råbte han efter tre infanterister uden geværer, der holdt skøderne af deres kapper op og smuttede forbi ham ind i Basar-passagen. »Stop, I slyngler!«
»Men hvordan vil du standse dem?« svarede en anden officer. »Der er ingen mulighed for at samle dem. Hæren burde rykke frem, før resten stikker af, det er det hele!«
»Hvordan kan man rykke frem? De sidder fast, kilet sammen på broen og rører sig ikke. Skulle vi ikke sætte en afspærring op for at forhindre resten i at løbe bort?«
»Kom, gå derind og driv dem ud!« råbte den øverste officer.

Officeren med sjalet steg af, tilkaldte en trommeslager og gik med ham ind i arkaden. Nogle soldater begyndte at løbe bort i en flok. En butiksindehaver med røde bumser på kinderne nær næsen og med et roligt, vedholdende, beregnende udtryk i sit fyldige ansigt nærmede sig hastigt og ivrigt officeren med svingende arme.

»Deres ære!« sagde han. »Vær så god at beskytte os! Vi er ikke nærige med småting, De er velkommen til hvad som helst — vi er kun glade! Vær så venlig!... Jeg henter straks et stykke klæde til en så ærværdig herre, eller endda to stykker med glæde. For vi forstår, hvordan det hænger sammen; men det her — det er det rene røveri! Hvis det behager Dem, kunne man ikke sætte vagter ud, bare så vi kan lukke butikken...«
Adskillige butiksindehavere stimlede sammen om officeren.
»Nå, hvilket vrøvl!« sagde en af dem, en mager, streng mand. »Når hovedet er væk, græder man ikke over håret! Tag hvad I vil!« Og han svingede sin arm energisk og vendte sig halvt om mod officeren.
»Det er let nok for dig at tale, Ivan Sidorytj!« sagde den første handlende vredt. »Vær venlig at træde indenfor, Deres ære!«
»Snak!« råbte den magre. »I mine tre butikker her har jeg varer for hundrede tusind rubler. Kan de reddes, når hæren er væk? Nå, sikke nogen folk! 'Mod Guds magt kan ingen kæmpe.'«
»Træd indenfor, Deres ære!« gentog den handlende med en bøjning.
Officeren stod ubeslutsom, og hans ansigt viste rådvildhed.
»Det er ikke min sag!« udbrød han og skridtede hurtigt ned ad en af passagerne.
Fra en åben butik lød slag og skældsord, og netop da officeren nåede hen til den, blev en mand i grå frakke med raget hoved voldsomt kastet ud.

Denne mand, foroverbøjet, styrtede forbi den handlende og officeren. Officeren kastede sig over de soldater, der var i butikkerne, men i det øjeblik nåede forfærdelige skrig dem fra den enorme folkemængde på Moskvabroen, og officeren løb ud på pladsen.
»Hvad er det? Hvad er det?« spurgte han, men hans kammerat galopperede allerede forbi Vasilij den Saliges kirke i den retning, hvorfra skrigene kom.

Officeren besteg sin hest og red efter ham. Da han nåede broen, så han to affuterede kanoner, infanteriet, der krydsede broen, adskillige væltede kærrer og forskrækkede og leende ansigter blandt tropperne. Ved kanonerne holdt en kærre med to forspændte heste. Fire mynder med halsbånd pressede sig tæt op mod hjulene. Kærren var læsset højt, og allerøverst sad en bondekone ved siden af en barnestol med benene i vejret og udstødte gennemtrængende, desperate skrig. Han fik af sine kammerater at vide, at folkemængdens skrig og kvindens hyl skyldtes, at general Jermolov, der var kommet hen til menneskemængden og havde fået at vide, at soldater spredtes mellem butikkerne, mens civile blokerede broen, havde befalet to kanoner affuteret og truet med at skyde mod broen. Folkemængden, der masede hinanden, væltede kærrer og skreg og pressede sig desperat sammen, havde ryddet broen, og tropperne rykkede nu fremad.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: The Russian troops passed through Moscow from two in the morning until two in the afternoon, carrying the wounded and the last departing residents with them.
The worst congestion occurred at the Stone, Moskva, and Yauza bridges.

While the troops, splitting into two streams around the Kremlin, crowded the Moskva and Stone bridges, a great many soldiers — taking advantage of the delay and gridlock — turned back from the bridges and slipped stealthily and silently past the Church of St. Basil, under the Borovitsky gate, and back up the hill to Red Square, where some instinct told them they could easily help themselves to things that weren't theirs. Crowds like those at a clearance sale filled every passage and alley of the Bazaar. But there were no dealers calling out with ingratiating affability, no hawkers, no usual motley crowd of female shoppers — only soldiers in uniforms and overcoats, though without muskets, entering the Bazaar empty-handed and silently making their way out through the passages with bundles. The shopkeepers and their assistants (of whom very few remained) moved about among the soldiers in bewilderment. They unlocked their shops and locked them again, and carried goods away themselves with the help of their assistants. On the square in front of the Bazaar, drummers beat the muster call. But the drumroll, instead of drawing looting soldiers toward it as it once would have, drove them farther away. Among the soldiers in the shops and passages, men in gray coats with shaved heads could be seen. Two officers — one with a scarf over his uniform mounted on a lean gray horse, the other in an overcoat and on foot — stood at the corner of Ilyinka Street, talking. A third officer galloped up.
"The general orders them all driven out immediately, without fail. This is outrageous! Half the men have scattered."
"Where are you going? Where?" he shouted at three infantrymen without muskets who, holding up the skirts of their overcoats, were slipping past into the Bazaar passage. "Stop, you rascals!"
"But how are you going to stop them?" another officer replied. "There's no rounding them up. The army needs to push on before the rest scatter — that's all!"
"How can we push on? They're stuck on the bridge, jammed solid. Shouldn't we throw a cordon around to keep the rest from running off?"
"Go in there and drive them out!" the senior officer shouted.

The officer in the scarf dismounted, called for a drummer, and went into the arcade. Some soldiers started running away in a group. A shopkeeper with red pimples on his cheeks near his nose, wearing a calm, patient, calculating expression on his plump face, hurried up to the officer, swinging his arms ostentatiously.

"Your honor!" he said. "Please be so kind as to protect us! We won't begrudge trifles — you're welcome to anything, we'd be delighted! Please! I'll fetch a piece of cloth right away for such a distinguished gentleman, or even two, with pleasure. Because we understand the situation — but this here is just plain robbery! If you please, sir, couldn't guards be posted, at least to let us close up shop?"
Several other shopkeepers crowded around the officer.

"Bah, what drivel!" said one of them — a thin, stern-looking man. "When your head's been cut off you don't weep for your hair! Take whatever you want!" And he waved his arm energetically and turned sideways to the officer.
"Easy for you to talk, Ivan Sidorych!" the first tradesman said angrily. "Please step inside, your honor!"

"Talk indeed!" the thin one retorted. "In my three shops I've got a hundred thousand rubles' worth of goods. Can they be saved once the army's gone? Well, people — 'against God's might our hands can't fight.'"
"Come inside, your honor!" the first tradesman repeated, bowing.
The officer stood there, perplexed, indecision on his face.
"It's none of my business!" he exclaimed, and strode quickly down one of the passages.
From one open shop came the sound of blows and cursing, and just as the officer reached it, a man in a gray coat with a shaved head was thrown violently out the door.

The man, doubled over, rushed past the tradesman and the officer. The officer grabbed at the soldiers who were in the shops, but at that moment terrible screams reached them from the huge crowd on the Moskva bridge, and the officer ran out to the square.
"What is it? What's happening?" he asked, but his fellow officer was already galloping past St. Basil's toward the source of the screams.

The officer mounted his horse and rode after him. When he reached the bridge he saw two unlimbered guns, infantry crossing, several overturned carts, and frightened, laughing faces among the troops. Beside the cannon stood a cart harnessed to two horses. Four greyhounds with collars pressed close to the wheels. The cart was piled high, and at the very top — beside a child's chair turned upside down — sat a peasant woman, shrieking piercingly. He was told by his fellow officers that the crowd's screams and the woman's shrieks were caused by General Ermolov, who had ridden up to the crowd and, learning that soldiers were looting the shops while civilians clogged the bridge, had ordered two guns unlimbered and made a show of firing at the bridge. The crowd, crushing one another, overturning carts, screaming and squeezing desperately, had cleared off the bridge, and the troops were now advancing.
